title: Two Strategies to Measure Spin-Orbit-Torque Efficiency Acting on the Insulating Magnet Li$_{0.5}$Al$_{0.7}$Fe$_{1.8}$O$_4$
authors: Orion Smedley, Thow Min Jerald Cham, Daisy O'Mahoney, Sanyum Channa, Xin Yu Zheng, Anna Janni, Lauren J. Riddiford, Yuhan Liang, Bozo Vareskic, Zbigniew Galazka, Yunqiu Kelly Luo, Yuri Suzuki, Daniel C. Ralph
abstract: For insulating magnets, widely-used electrically-based techniques to measure spin-orbit-torque efficiency can suffer from poor signal-to-noise ratios and unwanted artifacts, while optical measurements based on conventional magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) imaging often lack sufficient sensitivity. Here we analyze two strategies for measuring the spin-torque efficiency acting on an insulating magnet, focusing on the torque from Pt acting on thin films of the low-damping magnet lithium aluminum ferrite (LAFO). First, lateral + longitudinal spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) allows separation of the spin-torque signal from artifacts due to spin-pumping and resonant heating. With this technique, we measure a spin-torque efficiency $ξ^\text{ST-FMR}_\text{DL}\sim\ 0.07$, comparable to but a bit less than for Pt acting on metallic ferromagnets. Second, we attempted optical measurements of spin-orbit-torque-induced magnetic deflection using Sagnac interferometry. We find that Sagnac interferometry provides sufficient sensitivity to measure signals from 14.4 nm LAFO thin films, but the inferred torque efficiency is much weaker than the result from lateral + longitudinal ST-FMR. We speculate that there may be another contribution to the Sagnac signal other than current-induced magnetic deflection, perhaps an out-of-plane component of itinerant electron spins. This becomes relevant for insulating magnets in which the magneto-optic coupling coefficient is very weak.
summary: This work tackles the difficult measurement of spin-orbit-torque efficiency in insulating magnets using two advanced techniques: ST-FMR and Sagnac interferometry. ST-FMR yields a quantifiable efficiency value, while the optical method suggests a much weaker torque. The discrepancy prompts speculation about overlooked magnetic contributions, particularly out-of-plane spin components, crucial for understanding insulating spintronics.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing sensitive and reliable methods to measure the spin-orbit-torque (SOT) efficiency in insulating magnetic materials.
main_result: The authors report a spin-torque efficiency of $\xi_{\text{ST-FMR}} \sim 0.07$ using ST-FMR, which is comparable to metallic ferromagnets, while an optical measurement yielded a significantly weaker result, suggesting unaccounted physics in the optical setup.
method: Two complementary experimental strategies were employed: (1) Lateral + longitudinal Spin-Torque Ferromagnetic Resonance (ST-FMR) to extract torque coefficients, and (2) Sagnac interferometry to measure optically induced magnetic deflection.
model_or_system: The study focuses on thin films of the insulating magnet lithium aluminum ferrite ($	ext{Li}_{0.5}	ext{Al}_{0.7}	ext{Fe}_{1.8}	ext{O}_4$, LAFO) coated with a Pt layer. The analysis models magnetization dynamics under the influence of spin-orbit torque.
key_observables: Spin-torque efficiency ($\xi$), DC voltages ($	ext{V}_{XX}, 	ext{V}_{XY}$) from ST-FMR, and magnetic deflection angle ($\theta_k$) from Sagnac interferometry.
important_parameters: LAFO thickness ($14.4 \text{ nm}$), applied current density ($5.1(5) \times 10^{10} \text{ A m}^{-2}$), and the derived spin-torque efficiency values.
main_assumptions: The ST-FMR analysis assumes the separation of spin-torque signals from artifacts like spin-pumping and resonant heating. The optical analysis speculates that the discrepancy might arise from an out-of-plane spin component not captured by the standard model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	ext{XRD}$ and $	ext{SQUID}$ magnetometry of LAFO, the contact geometry, and $	ext{FMR}$ linewidth/resonance field measurements used for characterization.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty of measuring SOT in insulators. It then details the ST-FMR approach, deriving torque coefficients from measured voltages, and presents the resulting efficiency. Subsequently, it analyzes the Sagnac interferometry results, comparing them to the ST-FMR findings and discussing the physical implications of the discrepancy.
why_interesting: While the core physics is condensed matter magnetism, the comparison between electrical (ST-FMR) and optical (Sagnac) measurement techniques for quantifying fundamental coupling constants (like SOT efficiency) is highly relevant to experimental quantum sensing and characterization of magnetic states.

In panels d) and e) the magnetic field is oriented along the [001] direction.
